evidence.claim: The orchard landscape has roots in John S. Harris’s experiments at La Crescent.
evidence.quote: John S. Harris planted apple trees here, resulting in many orchards in the present-day city.

evidence.claim: He planted the area’s first apple trees in 1857, testing varieties until he found trees that could withstand Minnesota winters.
evidence.quote: Harris planted the area's first apple trees in 1857, experimenting until he grew trees hardy enough to withstand Minnesota winters.

evidence.claim: He planted thousands of trees and hundreds of varieties; he called half of them total failures.
evidence.quote: He planted thousands of apple trees and hundreds of varieties, a full half of which he said were total failures.

evidence.claim: Harris became a founding member of the Minnesota State Horticultural Society, and his planting helped establish the city’s orchard identity.
evidence.quote: Harris became known as "Father of the Orchardists" in Minnesota, and was a founding member of the Minnesota State Horticultural Society.

evidence.claim: Harris became a founding member of the Minnesota State Horticultural Society, and his planting helped establish the city’s orchard identity.

evidence.claim: Bluffs rise 500 feet above the Mississippi here, but establishing a park with river views proved difficult.
evidence.quote: The park preserves steep-sided bluffs rising 500 feet (150 m) above the river

evidence.claim: The first plan, authorized in 1963, called for a narrow strip between La Crescent and Dresbach.
evidence.quote: Legislation authorizing a 1,350-acre (546 ha) park was passed in 1963.  The layout was a long, narrow strip along the blufftops between La Crescent and Dresbach

evidence.claim: Landowners would not sell, and none of that land was acquired.
evidence.quote: they  proved unwilling to sell their river views, and none of the property was ever acquired.

evidence.claim: A transfer of state forest land farther north in 1971 gave the park a different home; it opened in 1976.
evidence.quote: Legislation in 1971 transferred 1,073 acres (434 ha) from the forestry division to the parks division

evidence.claim: Short trails reach river viewpoints and overlooks of steep grasslands known as goat prairies.
evidence.quote: Other short trails lead out to viewpoints, some of the Mississippi River and Wisconsin shore, and some to goat prairies overlooking a narrow valley.

evidence.claim: Steep terrain and fragile habitats limited development, leaving the park’s roads and trails winding along fairly level ridgetops.
evidence.quote: Development in the park was limited by the steep terrain and fragile habitats.  Thus the roads and trails snake along the ridgetops and are fairly level despite the varied topography.

evidence.claim: Dakota Creek meets the Mississippi at Dakota, a town with both ferry and fruit-growing history.
evidence.quote: Dakota Creek and the Mississippi River meet at Dakota.

evidence.claim: The town was laid out in 1855 and developed in 1859 by Nathan Brown, who operated a stockyard and a ferry to Wisconsin.
evidence.quote: It was laid out in 1855 and developed in 1859 by Nathan Brown, who came to Minnesota in 1847, had a stockyard, and ran a ferry service to Wisconsin.

evidence.claim: Berry growing once centered here; apple growing became the main industry.
evidence.quote: Once the center of berry growing, the main industry is now apple growing.

evidence.claim: County Road 12, part of the Apple Blossom Scenic Drive, is among the routes serving the town.
evidence.quote: Other routes include Winona County Road 12, the Apple Blossom Scenic Drive.

evidence.claim: Peter Cameron tried to bring the Mississippi closer to La Crescent by digging a canal that would bypass La Crosse across the river.
evidence.quote: he tried to dig a canal to change the flow of the Mississippi River so it would flow closer to La Crescent and bypass La Crosse, Wisconsin across the river.

evidence.claim: He and Emma Cameron had founded the town in 1851 under the name Camerons.
evidence.quote: La Crescent was founded in 1851 by Peter and Emma Cameron, who called it "Camerons".

evidence.claim: Peter died ten weeks before the canal’s scheduled completion in 1857, and the work was never finished.
evidence.quote: He died 10 weeks before its scheduled completion in 1857, and the canal was never finished

evidence.claim: The town’s later name came from the crescent-shaped bend of the Mississippi.
evidence.quote: came up with "La Crescent", after the bend or "crescent" shape of the Mississippi River around the town.

evidence.claim: The Great River Road passes through La Crescent on US 61 and a short section of Minnesota 16.
evidence.quote: passes through La Crescent via US 61 and a short piece of MN 16.

evidence.claim: The unfinished canal remains visible in aerial photographs of the city, a trace of Cameron’s attempt to alter the river’s course.
evidence.quote: the canal was never finished, although the canal can still be seen in aerial photographs of the city.
